newsitem.title: USA: Fog may postpone U.S. shuttle landing.
newsitem.headline: Fog may postpone U.S. shuttle landing.

text.p: Ground fog at Florida's spaceport threatened on Monday to delay the return to Earth of the space shuttle Discovery after a jam-packed, 11-day research mission, NASA officials said.

The $2 billion reusable spaceship was to land at the Florida's Kennedy Space Center at 7:14 a.m. EDT (1114 GMT), but forecasters feared fog could cut visibility at the landing strip to less than two miles, NASA mission commentator Kyle Herring said.

"That ground fog development could obscure the runway which would be a no-go situation," he said. "The weather officer reported it's going to be a nail-biter in terms of deciding whether we are going to bring Discovery home this morning."
The shuttle has only one landing slot on Monday because NASA officials passed up an early landing opportunity to avoid a more risky predawn touchdown.
The shuttle's back up landing strip at Edwards Air Force Base in California was not being considered on Monday. If fog delayed the shuttle's homecoming, NASA said it would try again on Tuesday.
The shuttle has enough fuel and supplies to stay aloft until Thursday, but would probably return to Earth on one coast or the other by Wednesday, flight director Wayne Hale said.

Discovery's clam-like cargo bay doors were closed at about 3:30 a.m. EDT (0730 GMT) in preparation for landing. The spaceship's braking rockets were due to fire about an hour before touchdown to start its descent.
Reentering the atmosphere over the South Pacific, the shuttle will make a rare southerly approach to the Florida peninsula that will take it over Central America and close to the shoreline of Cuba.

Discovery's crew of six, which includes a Canadian guest researcher, were to return with an atmospheric satellite carrying a bounty of information on the depletion of the Earth's protective ozone layer.

During a busy 11-day mission, the astronauts tested a Japanese prototype space station robot arm, grew colon cancer cells for medical research, and pointed a telescope at the receding Comet Hale-Bopp.

As Discovery's astronauts prepared to come home, the space shuttle Atlantis, meanwhile, was being rolled to its seaside launch pad at the Kennedy Space Center for a planned late-September launch to Russia's Mir space station.
